newsitem.title: INDONESIA: East Timor quiet on Good Friday, no fresh protest.
newsitem.headline: East Timor quiet on Good Friday, no fresh protest.

text.p: The troubled Indonesia-ruled territory of East Timor was quiet on Good Friday, but police were deployed in the capital Dili in an apparent move to prevent disturbances, residents said.

Roman Catholic East Timor was rocked last Sunday when a group of youths held an anti-Indonesia protest at a Dili hotel where the U.N. special envoy for East Timor Jamsheed Marker was staying during a familiarisation visit.
At least 11 people were injured when police broke up the protest and 24 people were arrested on charges of showing hatred against Indonesia.
"It's quiet today. People went to church this morning for Good Friday mass and returned to their houses peacefully," local legislator Manuel Carascalao told Reuters by telephone.
"Police presence is obvious in the city since yesterday. I saw trucks carrying anti-riot police patrolling in the city and I think it is a move to prevent unrest," he added.
Police were not available for comment. Good Friday is a holiday in Indonesia, a Moslem-majority nation which recognises five major religions.
Other residents also said Dili was quiet and that 1996 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Bishop Carlos Belo celebrated mass in the capital on Thursday.

"I don't think there are going to be disturbances today or on Sunday. I don't think East Timorese will spoil Good Friday and the Easter celebration on Sunday with protests or stuff like that," said a resident.
Police have said they had detained 24 East Timorese and charged them with showing hatred against the Indonesian government after Sunday's protest, when they demanded a meeting with Marker.

Residents said demonstrators, mainly students, tried to meet Marker after they felt he was only meeting government officials and Belo. Marker denied he had refused to meet the students, saying they had not asked for a meeting.
But in Jakarta, a group of East Timorese youths managed to secure a meeting with Marker on Tuesday after entering the Austrian embassy hours earlier.
They asked the embassy officials to help arrange a meeting with him. The Timorese were questioned by the police after they left the embassy early on Thursday.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 and annexed it the following year in a move not recognised by the United Nations.

Residents estimate that between 200,000 and 250,000 people have been killed in the invasion, a subsequent famine and the two decades that Indonesia has tried to put down the insurrection in the territory.
